articles.title: Enforcing ADRs with Deterministic Architecture Tests
articles.excerpt: TL;DR: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) turn into dead documentation the moment a team accumulates more than thirty decisions. I stop this architectural drift by enforcing rules deterministically:…
articles.body: TL;DR: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) turn into dead documentation the moment a team accumulates more than thirty decisions. I stop this architectural drift by enforcing rules deterministically: automated architecture tests fail the build on broken boundaries, a one-line context index keeps rules inside human and AI context limits, and explicit anti-pattern definitions catch what static tests cannot. When I first introduced Architecture Decision Records (ADRs) to my team, I was thrilled with the result. We had a clean folder in the repository, markdown templates, and thoughtful discussions about boundaries and conventions. I even wrote about how team alignment sessions and ADRs helped us standardize our APIs in /nodes/standardizing-api-conventions/ . Then reality caught up with us.
articles.author: Roy Berris

articles.title: Before I let an agent open PRs on strangers' repos, I made it earn it
articles.excerpt: Over the last six weeks I've had 44 bug fixes merged into other people's open-source projects, most of them MCP servers. Many came from the same loop: mcp-doctor, my static linter for MCP servers, fla…
articles.body: Over the last six weeks I've had 44 bug fixes merged into other people's open-source projects, most of them MCP servers. Many came from the same loop: mcp-doctor , my static linter for MCP servers, flags something. I reproduce it, write the fix and a regression test, run the project's tests, and open a PR in their template. That loop is mechanical enough that an agent could run it. It's also the kind of thing you shouldn't hand to an agent on vibes. A wrong PR on a stranger's repo costs more than no PR: it takes a maintainer's time, and it spends my reputation. So before building the agent, I wrote down the bar it had to clear. This post covers how it cleared it, where it failed, and the bug it caught in my own tool on its first real run.

articles.body: I built GitPixelPush to turn a GitHub contribution calendar into a drawing canvas. It is a creative experiment: the generated activity is clearly labeled artwork. What you can try Open the demo canvas, sketch a pattern, stamp text, or use a preset. The preview shows the planned dates and commit count before you decide to connect GitHub and push. Publishing creates backdated empty commits in a repository you choose. The commit labels and repository README disclose their purpose. These squares do not represent software development or prove anyone’s productivity. The permission tradeoff GitHub authorization deserves attention even for a playful tool. Public canvases use public-repository access; private canvases require a broader scope.

articles.title: Null Is Not Zero: What an MCP Tool Description Has to Carry
articles.excerpt: A REST API's documentation is read by a developer once. An MCP tool description is the one piece of text a model reads on every single call, which makes it where you stop an agent misreporting your nu…
articles.body: A REST API's documentation is read by a developer once. An MCP tool description is the one piece of text a model reads on every single call, which makes it where you stop an agent misreporting your numbers. It is also prose, so it goes stale like prose. AddressIntel reads building permits and parcel records across the SF Peninsula and scores what could be built on a given lot. It already had a REST API. Putting a Model Context Protocol server in front of that API is, as engineering, close to trivial: the whole thing is 312 lines of TypeScript across two files, six tools, and a client that adds a header, builds a query string and unwraps the API's error envelope. What is not trivial is that the consumer changed.

articles.title: Conversational AI vs Generative AI: Key Differences Explained
articles.excerpt: TL;DR Conversational AI is an interaction system. Generative AI is a capability for creating or transforming content. A product can use either one without the other, or combine both. Traditional conve…
articles.body: TL;DR Conversational AI is an interaction system. Generative AI is a capability for creating or transforming content. A product can use either one without the other, or combine both. Traditional conversational systems emphasize intent recognition, state, business rules, and deterministic fulfillment. Generative systems emphasize context, model behavior, grounding, evaluation, and output controls. The hybrid pattern is common in production: a conversation layer manages identity and state, an LLM interprets or drafts, retrieval provides approved knowledge, and ordinary services execute authorized actions. Test the whole path. A fluent answer is still a product failure if it uses the wrong account, loses conversation state, cites stale knowledge, or performs an unauthorized action.

articles.title: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.excerpt: On this day in space! Oct. 14, 1947: Test pilot Chuck Yeager breaks the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, the first X-plane
articles.body: On Oct. 14, 1947, Chuck Yeager broke the sound barrier for the first time! Chuck Yeager was a test pilot for the U.S. Air Force who made history by flying an aircraft faster than the speed of sound. Yeager made his historic flight in a Bell X-1 rocket plane that he named "Glamorous Glennis" after his wife. Yeager had broken two ribs the night before when he fell off a horse, but that didn't stop him! His aircraft was dropped from a Boeing B-29 bomber before accelerating to a speed of Mach 1.07, which is about 821 mph (1,321 km/h). The speed of sound, Mach 1, is about 760 mph (1,223 km/h). USAF Capt. Charles E. Yeager (shown standing with the Bell X-1 supersonic rocket plane) became the first man to fly faster than the speed of sound in level flight on Oct. 14, 1947.

articles.body: Don't expect any of the Artemis II moon astronauts to fly again soon. On Tuesday (Oct. 13), NASA announced that Artemis II mission specialist Christina Koch will become the agency’s acting deputy chief engineer, effective Nov. 1. "With this appointment, Koch will transition to management astronaut status and will no longer be eligible for future spaceflight assignments," NASA officials wrote in a statement on Tuesday . Her three Artemis II crewmates had already shared their next moves, none of which put another spaceflight in play in the near future. Mission commander Reid Wiseman and pilot Victor Glover , both of NASA, became "emeritus" astronauts last month, a role that seems to include planning, advising and mentoring duties but no flights into the final frontier.

On October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K.

articles.excerpt: A "jellyfish" in the early-morning sky created by SpaceX's launch of the CRS-35 cargo mission on Oct. 13, 2026.
articles.body: A "jellyfish" in the early-morning sky created by SpaceX's launch of the CRS-35 cargo mission on Oct. 13, 2026. (Image credit: SpaceX) Did you see a gigantic, glowing jellyfish in the night sky early on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13)? If so, it's not an alien invasion (sorry); it was SpaceX launching its latest mission to the International Space Station (ISS). What is it? Just before dawn on Tuesday (Oct. 13), a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket lifted off from Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida, carrying to space a robotic Dragon capsule filled with thousands of pounds of cargo. The liftoff kicked off CRS-35, the 35th mission that SpaceX is flying to the ISS as part of the company's Commercial Resupply Services agreement with NASA.

articles.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
articles.excerpt: "Small weight-based replicators" could usher in a new generation of computer worms.
articles.body: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered.
